inputs.system:
You are BIE's book-understanding section: an expert teacher of Science and Technology for UPSC / State PCS aspirants preparing for UPSC / State PCS.
You read one page of a book chapter with two eyes, the page's native text blocks and the page image, and turn it into a complete,
question-based teacher's understanding. Later BIE sections build the video lessons, the chapter game and the notes only from what you
capture, so anything you miss is missing from the whole course.

Course: "10. Tissues and Its Types" · subject: Science and Technology · learners: UPSC / State PCS aspirants · exam: UPSC / State PCS · learner language: Hinglish.
Your output is internal to BIE: write it in clear English and keep the book's own terms and spellings.

Navin's rules for this section (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never shorten work to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, completeness wins.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. Keep outside explanations at standard textbook level for these learners and avoid absolute words (always, only, never, all, every) unless the book uses them.
[S1-08] Give every item its true content type (definition, fact, process, structure, comparison, classification, timeline, cause_effect, formula, data, example, question). The content type decides later how the video shows it, how the game makes it playable and how the notes draw it, so choose by what the content is, not by how it is printed.
[S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.
[S1-11] Where the text layer and the image disagree (garbled symbols, missing words, wrong order), report the disagreement. Trust the image for symbols, layout and diagrams, and the text layer for spelling when it is clean.

How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part) with a reason each, and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "".
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the list given.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree).
  - content_type: what the content really is (definition, fact, process, structure, comparison, classification, timeline, cause_effect,
    formula, data, example, question, other).
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (see S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside". BIE's code checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how"; a process needs "how"; a comparison or classification needs "compare" or
    "difference".
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.
- text_image_disagreements: where the text layer and the image differ.
Reply with the JSON object only.

output.page_summary: Sclerenchyma consists of dead, long and narrow, heavily lignified cells with no intercellular spaces; it occurs around stem vascular bundles, in leaf veins, and in hard seed and nut coverings, providing protection and mechanical strength. Complex permanent tissues contain coordinated cell types and transport water, minerals and food. Xylem and phloem are the two types. Xylem contains tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres: tubular conducting elements support vertical transport, parenchyma stores food and conducts water sideways, and fibres provide support. The illustrations show these components and introduce phloem structures including sieve tubes, companion cells, sieve plates and plasmodesmata.

items.content: 3. Sclerenchyma Tissue
items.exam_note: A major plant tissue identification topic.

items.content: Occurrence:
items.exam_note: Organises the following locations.

items.content: • In stems around vascular bundles.

teacher_understanding.question: Where in stems does this page locate sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Around the vascular bundles, rather than simply somewhere unspecified in the stem.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is sclerenchyma useful around vascular bundles?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its thick, lignified walls reinforce the region containing conducting tissues and help it resist mechanical deformation.

items.exam_note: Match tissue with its position around vascular bundles.

items.content: • In veins of leaves.

teacher_understanding.question: Which part of the leaf is listed as a location of sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: The veins of leaves.

teacher_understanding.question: How does sclerenchyma contribute to the leaf vein's role?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its rigid walls add mechanical reinforcement to the vein region, helping support the leaf blade.

items.exam_note: A location-based tissue identification fact.

items.content: • Hard covering of seeds and nuts.

teacher_understanding.question: Which protective plant coverings contain sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: The hard coverings of seeds and nuts.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does sclerenchyma suit a hard protective covering?
teacher_understanding.answer: Thick, lignified walls resist mechanical damage and contribute hardness to the covering.

items.exam_note: Connect hardness and protection with sclerenchyma.

items.content: Eg. Husk of coconut.

teacher_understanding.question: Which familiar material is given as an example of sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: The husk of coconut.

teacher_understanding.question: How does coconut husk help explain the mechanical role of sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its tough fibres provide a familiar example of the resistance and strength produced by thick-walled sclerenchyma cells.

items.exam_note: Classic example and odd-one-out material; retain 'husk', not a substituted plant part.

items.content: Structure:
items.exam_note: Introduces sclerenchyma structural features.

items.content:  Long and narrow

teacher_understanding.question: What cell shape does the page attribute to sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Long and narrow cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How should a teacher interpret this description without overgeneralising?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes the elongated fibre form particularly well. Sclerenchyma also includes sclereids with other shapes, so long and narrow should not be presented as the shape of every sclerenchyma cell.

items.exam_note: Recognise the book's description while avoiding an absolute shape rule.

items.content:  Walls are thickened by LIGNINS

teacher_understanding.question: What thickens the sclerenchyma walls according to the book?
teacher_understanding.answer: LIGNINS.

teacher_understanding.question: How does lignification support the function of sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Lignin deposition strengthens and stiffens the cell wall, making the tissue suited to mechanical support rather than easy stretching.

items.exam_note: Lignified walls are a key diagnostic feature.

items.content:  Cell cavity is absent due to excessive thickness.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the page describe the cell cavity as absent?
teacher_understanding.answer: It attributes the absence of the cavity to excessive thickness of the cell wall.

teacher_understanding.question: How should this statement be explained anatomically?
teacher_understanding.answer: Wall thickening reduces the internal cavity, called the lumen. Sclerenchyma commonly has a very narrow lumen rather than a universally absent cavity, so the printed wording is a simplification.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a cell cavity differ from an intercellular space?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cavity or lumen is inside an individual cell wall; an intercellular space lies between neighbouring cells.

items.exam_note: Distinguish lumen reduction from absence of spaces between cells; do not universalise the printed simplification.

items.content:  Intercellular spaces absent.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the page say about spaces between sclerenchyma cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: Intercellular spaces are absent.

teacher_understanding.question: How does close packing contribute to a supporting tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Closely packed, thick-walled cells form a compact reinforcing tissue rather than a tissue with conspicuous gaps between its cells.

items.exam_note: Important comparative structural character.

items.content:  Cells are dead.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the living status of sclerenchyma cells described here?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are dead cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How can a dead cell still support a plant?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mechanical support can be supplied by the persistent thick cell wall even after the living cell contents have been lost at maturity.

items.exam_note: Living-versus-dead tissue comparisons are frequently tested.

items.content: Function:
items.exam_note: Introduces sclerenchyma functions.

items.content: • Provide strength to plant cell.

teacher_understanding.question: What function does the first sclerenchyma function bullet state?
teacher_understanding.answer: Providing strength to the plant cell.

teacher_understanding.question: How is this strength produced?
teacher_understanding.answer: The thick, lignified wall resists deformation, and groups of such cells reinforce plant tissues.

items.exam_note: Link wall structure to strength.

items.content: • Provides protection and mechanical strength

teacher_understanding.question: Which two roles does the second function bullet associate with sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Protection and mechanical strength.

teacher_understanding.question: How do the listed locations illustrate these roles?
teacher_understanding.answer: Hard seed and nut coverings illustrate protection, while sclerenchyma around stem bundles and in leaf veins illustrates reinforcement and support.

items.exam_note: Match locations and structural properties with function.

items.content: COMPLEX PERMANENT TISSUE
items.exam_note: Introduces vascular tissue classification.

items.where_on_page: first bullet under complex permanent tissue
items.content: • Made up of more than one type of cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What makes a permanent tissue complex?
teacher_understanding.answer: It contains more than one type of cell.

teacher_understanding.question: How does complex permanent tissue differ from simple permanent tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Complex permanent tissue combines different cell types; simple permanent tissue is composed of one basic cell type.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is 'complex' not merely a description of how complicated a cell looks?
teacher_understanding.answer: The term classifies the tissue by the diversity of its constituent cell types, not by the appearance of an individual cell.

items.exam_note: Core definition for simple-versus-complex tissue questions.

items.where_on_page: second bullet under complex permanent tissue
items.content: • Cells co-ordinate to perform common function.

teacher_understanding.question: What unites the different cell types in a complex tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: They coordinate to perform a common function.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the xylem discussion illustrate this coordination?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tracheids and vessels conduct water and minerals, parenchyma stores food and helps sideways water conduction, and fibres support the tissue. Different roles contribute to the functioning of the same tissue.

items.exam_note: Understand coordination, not just the presence of multiple cell types.

items.content: Functions:
items.exam_note: Introduces the collective transport function.

items.content: • Transport water, minerals and food materials.

teacher_understanding.question: Which materials do complex permanent tissues transport?
teacher_understanding.answer: Water, minerals and food materials.

teacher_understanding.question: How should this collective function be divided between the two tissue types?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem chiefly conducts water and minerals, while phloem conducts food materials. The collective statement does not mean that each tissue performs every listed transport role in the same way.

items.exam_note: Avoid assigning the combined transport list indiscriminately to either tissue.

items.content:
Two types:
1. Xylem
2. Phloem

teacher_understanding.question: Which two types of complex permanent tissue are listed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem and phloem.

teacher_understanding.question: What classification feature do xylem and phloem share?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both belong to complex permanent tissue, whose different cell types coordinate in a common function.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is xylem not classified as simple tissue even though it has a common transport role?
teacher_understanding.answer: A common role does not imply a single cell type: the page names tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres as its constituents.

items.exam_note: Fundamental classification and odd-one-out material.

items.where_on_page: middle right, paired green and brown illustration
items.content: Diagram titled 'Complex Permanent Tissue'. Two adjacent, unconnected tissue drawings compare Xylem on the left with Phloem on the right. The xylem drawing labels Xylem Parenchyma, Vessels, Tracheids and Xylem Fibres. The phloem drawing labels Phloem Parenchyma, Companion cell, Phloem fibres and Sieve tube. Leader arrows identify parts; they do not show a direction of transport.

teacher_understanding.question: What does this paired diagram compare?
teacher_understanding.answer: The constituent structures of xylem and phloem, shown as the two complex permanent tissues.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the arrows be read?
teacher_understanding.answer: They connect anatomical structures to their names. They are label pointers, not arrows showing water or food flow.

items.exam_note: Use for visual recognition and component matching.

items.content: Complex Permanent Tissue
items.exam_note: Names the shared tissue category.

items.where_on_page: upper diagram, top label of left drawing
items.content: Xylem Parenchyma — pointer identifies the parenchyma component of the xylem drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: Which xylem component does this label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem parenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this component contribute to xylem function?
teacher_understanding.answer: It stores food and helps conduct water sideways.

items.exam_note: Match parenchyma with storage and lateral conduction.

items.where_on_page: upper diagram, second label of left drawing
items.content: Vessels — pointer identifies a tubular conducting component in the xylem drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: Which conducting component is identified here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Vessels.

teacher_understanding.question: How does their tubular structure relate to function?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page links tubular structure with vertical transport of water and minerals.

items.exam_note: Recognise a water-conducting component.

items.where_on_page: upper diagram, third label of left drawing
items.content: Tracheids — pointer identifies an elongated conducting cell in the xylem drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: Which xylem cells are named by this pointer?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tracheids.

teacher_understanding.question: How are tracheids related to vertical transport?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page groups them with vessels as tubular structures transporting water and minerals vertically.

items.exam_note: Identify tracheids as xylem conducting elements.

items.where_on_page: upper diagram, lowest label of left drawing
items.content: Xylem Fibres — pointer identifies the supporting fibre component in xylem.

teacher_understanding.question: Which component is identified by the lowest xylem pointer?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: How do these fibres contribute to xylem?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are mainly supportive in function.

items.exam_note: Distinguish support from the main conducting roles.

items.content: Xylem — identifies the entire left-hand tissue drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue is the left-hand drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem.

teacher_understanding.question: How is this drawing distinguished from the phloem drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: It labels tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres rather than sieve tube and companion-cell structures.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the collection of different labelled components matter?
teacher_understanding.answer: It illustrates why xylem is a complex permanent tissue rather than one cell type.

items.exam_note: Whole-tissue visual identification.

items.where_on_page: upper diagram, highest label of right drawing
items.content: Phloem Parenchyma — pointer identifies the parenchyma component at the outer side of the phloem drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: Which phloem component does the upper pointer identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: Phloem parenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the word parenchyma be interpreted here?
teacher_understanding.answer: It names a cell type within the complex tissue, not a claim that the whole phloem is simple parenchyma tissue.

items.exam_note: Recognise parenchyma as a component of phloem as well as xylem.

items.where_on_page: upper diagram, second label of right drawing
items.content: Companion cell — pointer identifies the elongated cell beside the sieve tube.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the labelled companion cell relative to the sieve tube?
teacher_understanding.answer: Beside the sieve tube in the phloem drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a companion cell help a sieve-tube element?
teacher_understanding.answer: It provides metabolic support and participates in the transfer of sugars into or out of the sieve-tube system.

items.exam_note: Companion cell is a strong phloem-identification clue.

items.where_on_page: upper diagram, third label of right drawing
items.content: Phloem fibres — pointer identifies an elongated fibre in the phloem drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: Which fibre component appears in the phloem diagram?
teacher_understanding.answer: Phloem fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: How do fibres contribute to a conducting tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their thick walls provide mechanical support; being part of a conducting tissue does not make each component a main food-conducting cell.

items.exam_note: Distinguish tissue membership from transport function.

items.where_on_page: upper diagram, lowest label of right drawing
items.content: Sieve tube — pointer identifies the broad central tube with cross-walls in the phloem drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the sieve-tube pointer identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: The broad tubular component with visible cross-walls in the phloem illustration.

teacher_understanding.question: How is a sieve tube constructed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sieve-tube elements are arranged end to end, with perforated sieve plates connecting successive elements for movement of phloem sap.

items.exam_note: Identify the characteristic conducting structure of phloem.

items.content: Phloem — identifies the entire right-hand tissue drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: Which tissue is the right-hand drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: Phloem.

teacher_understanding.question: Which labels distinguish this drawing from xylem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sieve tube and companion cell are characteristic labels here, along with phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: How can a student identify phloem without relying on its drawn colour?
teacher_understanding.answer: Use the sieve-tube and companion-cell arrangement; the illustration's colours are not a biological classification criterion.

items.exam_note: Identify tissues by structure rather than illustration colour.

items.content: Xylem structure. Pink drawings show a separate vessel-element example with pitted walls; a cluster of elongated tracheids with pitted walls; and a grouped view containing a xylem parenchyma cell, vessel element and tracheid. Leader lines associate the labels with the respective cells or walls. Small a. and b. markers distinguish illustrated views; there are no process-flow arrows.

teacher_understanding.question: What additional structural detail does the lower xylem panel show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows vessel elements and tracheids with pitted walls and a grouped view including xylem parenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this help connect cell form with water conduction?
teacher_understanding.answer: The elongated cells provide conducting pathways, while pits are regions through which water can move between adjacent conducting cells.

items.exam_note: Recognise vessel elements, tracheids and pitted walls.

items.where_on_page: top of lower boxed left panel
items.content: Xylem structure
items.exam_note: Panel title.

items.content: vessel elements — pointer identifies the separate pink vessel-element illustration.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the separate far-left xylem cell labelled?
teacher_understanding.answer: Vessel elements.

teacher_understanding.question: How is a vessel element related to a vessel?
teacher_understanding.answer: A vessel element is an individual cell unit; successive vessel elements join end to end to form a vessel.

items.exam_note: Distinguish an element from the multicellular vessel.

items.where_on_page: lower xylem panel, beside far-left vessel element
items.content: pitted walls — pointer identifies pits in the wall of the separate vessel-element drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does this label locate pits?
teacher_understanding.answer: In the wall of the vessel-element drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: How do pits assist water movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are regions where secondary wall thickening is absent, allowing water to pass through the remaining pit membrane between neighbouring cells.

items.exam_note: Pits are not simply unrestricted holes through the entire wall.

items.content: tracheids — label identifies the cluster of long, narrow pink cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Which cells form the labelled middle cluster?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tracheids.

teacher_understanding.question: How does water pass from one tracheid to another?
teacher_understanding.answer: Water moves through pits in their adjoining walls rather than through the open end-to-end perforations characteristic of vessel elements.

items.exam_note: Useful vessel-versus-tracheid distinction.

items.where_on_page: lower xylem panel, beside middle tracheid cluster
items.content: pitted walls — pointer identifies the wall pits of the tracheid cluster.

teacher_understanding.question: Which cells have pitted walls at this second pointer?
teacher_understanding.answer: The tracheids.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are pits important in otherwise thick-walled tracheids?
teacher_understanding.answer: They provide pathways for water exchange across neighbouring cell walls despite the extensive secondary wall thickening elsewhere.

items.exam_note: Pitted walls occur in both illustrated conducting cell types.

items.where_on_page: lower xylem panel, top of grouped right-hand view
items.content: xylem parenchyma cell — pointer identifies the slender parenchyma cell beside the vessel element.

teacher_understanding.question: Which non-vessel cell is identified beside the grouped vessel element?
teacher_understanding.answer: A xylem parenchyma cell.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this cell's role differ from the main conducting elements?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page assigns parenchyma food storage and sideways water conduction, while tracheids and vessels provide vertical water and mineral transport.

items.exam_note: Connect the labelled cell with storage and lateral transport.

items.where_on_page: lower xylem panel, grouped right-hand view, upper pointer
items.content: vessel element — pointer identifies the broader tubular cell in the grouped xylem view.

teacher_understanding.question: Which cell is labelled in the grouped view?
teacher_understanding.answer: A vessel element.

teacher_understanding.question: How does grouping it beside other cell types clarify xylem organisation?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows that the water-conducting element occurs alongside other constituents rather than constituting the entire tissue on its own.

items.exam_note: Recognise conducting elements within mixed-cell tissue.

items.where_on_page: lower xylem panel, below grouped right-hand view
items.content: tracheid — pointer identifies a narrow elongated cell in the grouped xylem view.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the bottom label in the grouped xylem view name?
teacher_understanding.answer: A tracheid.

teacher_understanding.question: How is a tracheid's function related to that of the neighbouring vessel element?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both are identified by the page as tubular structures involved in vertical transport of water and minerals.

items.exam_note: Identify the second conducting cell type in a mixed view.

items.content: Phloem structure. Blue drawings show a slender sieve-tube-element view with a sieve plate, an adjacent companion cell and a labelled nucleus, followed by a grouped view with companion cell, sieve-tube element, sieve plate, phloem parenchyma cells and plasmodesmata. The label 'phloem parenchyma cells' also appears beside the slender view. Leader lines identify structures; no transport-flow arrows are shown.

teacher_understanding.question: What finer phloem structures are visible in this panel?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sieve-tube elements, sieve plates, companion cells, a nucleus, phloem parenchyma cells and plasmodesmata.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the panel help explain phloem as a coordinated tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: It places conducting elements beside supporting living cells and labels their connecting structures, showing that the tissue is more than a single tube.

items.exam_note: Important visual vocabulary for phloem structure.

items.where_on_page: top of lower boxed right panel
items.content: Phloem structure
items.exam_note: Panel title.

items.where_on_page: lower phloem panel, top of slender left view
items.content: sieve plate — pointer identifies the end plate at the top of the slender sieve-tube-element drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the sieve plate labelled in the slender drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: At the end of the sieve-tube element.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a sieve plate enable continuity between sieve-tube elements?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its pores permit phloem sap to pass between successive elements.

items.exam_note: Locate sieve plates at junctions between sieve-tube elements.

items.where_on_page: lower phloem panel, upper left of slender view
items.content: sieve-tube element — pointer identifies the elongated conducting element in the slender view.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the elongated phloem conducting unit labelled?
teacher_understanding.answer: A sieve-tube element.

teacher_understanding.question: How is a sieve-tube element related to a sieve tube?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is one cellular unit in an end-to-end series forming a sieve tube.

items.exam_note: Distinguish individual element from complete tube.

items.where_on_page: lower phloem panel, left of slender view
items.content: companion cell — pointer identifies the small cell alongside the sieve-tube element.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the companion cell shown?
teacher_understanding.answer: Alongside the sieve-tube element.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is close association with a companion cell important?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mature sieve-tube elements have reduced cellular machinery, and the companion cell helps maintain their metabolism and food-transport activity.

items.exam_note: Recognise the paired sieve-tube-element and companion-cell arrangement.

items.where_on_page: lower phloem panel, left of lower part of slender view
items.content: phloem parenchyma cells — label names the parenchyma component beside the slender phloem view.

teacher_understanding.question: Which additional cell type is named beside this phloem view?
teacher_understanding.answer: Phloem parenchyma cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How do parenchyma cells contribute to phloem?
teacher_understanding.answer: They participate in storage and local transfer of organic materials within the tissue.

items.exam_note: Recognise another constituent of complex phloem tissue.

items.where_on_page: lower phloem panel, right of slender view
items.content: nucleus — pointer identifies the dark body within the companion-cell region beside the sieve-tube element.

teacher_understanding.question: What cellular structure does the nucleus label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: The dark body in the companion-cell region adjacent to the conducting element.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must the nucleus not be assigned indiscriminately to a mature sieve-tube element?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mature sieve-tube elements lack a nucleus, whereas companion cells retain one. This distinction helps explain their close functional association.

items.exam_note: Avoid confusing companion-cell nuclei with mature sieve-tube-element contents.

items.where_on_page: lower phloem panel, above grouped right view
items.content: companion cell — pointer identifies a cell alongside the sieve-tube elements in the grouped view.

teacher_understanding.question: Which associated cell is identified above the grouped view?
teacher_understanding.answer: A companion cell.

teacher_understanding.question: How is this repeated label useful for visual recognition?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows the same cell association in a grouped tissue view as in the separate view: the companion cell lies beside a sieve-tube element.

items.exam_note: Recognise the same structure in different views.

items.where_on_page: lower phloem panel, upper right of grouped view
items.content: sieve-tube element — pointer identifies a broad conducting unit within the grouped phloem view.

teacher_understanding.question: Which conducting unit is identified in the grouped view?
teacher_understanding.answer: A sieve-tube element.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the grouped view relate it to its neighbours?
teacher_understanding.answer: It places it next to companion and parenchyma cells and shows the sieve plate between conducting units.

items.exam_note: Identify conducting units within a tissue-level drawing.

items.where_on_page: lower phloem panel, middle right of grouped view
items.content: sieve plate — pointer identifies the transverse junction between sieve-tube elements in the grouped view.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the sieve plate in the grouped view?
teacher_understanding.answer: At a transverse junction between sieve-tube elements.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a sieve plate differ from an impermeable partition?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its pores allow sap movement from one element into the next rather than sealing the conducting pathway.

items.exam_note: Recognise the perforated end-wall junction.

items.where_on_page: lower phloem panel, below grouped view, left label
items.content: phloem parenchyma cells — pointer identifies the parenchyma cells in the grouped phloem view.

teacher_understanding.question: Which cells are named below the left side of the grouped view?
teacher_understanding.answer: Phloem parenchyma cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should these not be confused with the sieve-tube elements?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are a different constituent cell type, contributing storage and local transfer rather than forming the main longitudinal sieve-tube pathway.

items.exam_note: Separate phloem component identities and functions.

items.where_on_page: lower phloem panel, below grouped view, right label
items.content: plasmo-desmata — line-broken label points to connections between neighbouring cells in the grouped phloem view.

teacher_understanding.question: What connecting structure is labelled at the bottom right?
teacher_understanding.answer: Plasmodesmata, printed across two lines as 'plasmo-' and 'desmata'.

teacher_understanding.question: How do plasmodesmata connect plant cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are cytoplasmic channels through cell walls that allow communication and movement of substances between neighbouring living cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How do plasmodesmata differ from the sieve plate labelled nearby?
teacher_understanding.answer: Plasmodesmata are intercellular cytoplasmic channels; a sieve plate is the specialised porous end wall between successive sieve-tube elements.

items.exam_note: Useful structural distinction; no transport rates or quantitative claims are given.

items.content:  Xylem consists of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: What four components make up xylem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: How do these components differ in their stated functions?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tracheids and vessels transport water and minerals vertically; parenchyma stores food and helps sideways water conduction; fibres are mainly supportive.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is remembering only vessels an incomplete understanding of xylem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem is a coordinated complex tissue with conducting, storage, lateral-conduction and supporting components, not just a vessel.

items.exam_note: Four-part composition is central to matching and odd-one-out questions.

items.content:  Tracheids and vessels have thick walls, and many are dead cells when mature.

teacher_understanding.question: Which wall and maturity features does the book state for tracheids and vessels?
teacher_understanding.answer: They have thick walls, and the page says many are dead cells when mature.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are thick walls useful in water-conducting elements?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their lignified secondary walls help resist collapse as water is pulled through the xylem under tension.

teacher_understanding.question: How can cells conduct water after losing their living contents?
teacher_understanding.answer: Water moves through their remaining lumens and connecting wall pathways. Loss of the protoplast leaves a conducting space; living contents are not required inside each mature conducting element for this bulk flow.

items.exam_note: Retain the page's qualifier 'many'; distinguish conducting elements from the entire xylem tissue.

items.where_on_page: bottom text, third bullet across two lines
items.content:  Tracheids and vessels are tubular structures. This allows them to transport water and minerals vertically.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the page relate the shape of tracheids and vessels to their function?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their tubular form allows vertical transport of water and minerals.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a tube useful but not a sufficient explanation of what drives transport?
teacher_understanding.answer: A tube supplies a pathway. The main upward movement is driven by transpiration pull acting through a connected column of water, with other contributions such as root pressure under some conditions.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this direction of transport compare with the parenchyma role stated next?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tracheids and vessels are linked to vertical transport, while xylem parenchyma helps sideways conduction of water.

items.exam_note: Important structure–function and direction-of-conduction link.

items.content:  The parenchyma stores food and help in sideways conduction of water.

teacher_understanding.question: What two functions are assigned to xylem parenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: Storage of food and assistance in sideways conduction of water.

teacher_understanding.question: How should sideways conduction be visualised?
teacher_understanding.answer: As lateral movement across the tissue or between nearby regions, rather than transport along the plant's length.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does food storage in xylem not make xylem the main food-transport tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Storage is different from long-distance transport. A tissue may contain storage cells while its main conducting elements chiefly move water and minerals.

items.exam_note: High-value exception to the oversimplification that every xylem cell merely conducts water vertically.

items.content:  Xylem fibres are mainly supportive in function.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the main function of xylem fibres?
teacher_understanding.answer: Support.

teacher_understanding.question: How do xylem fibres provide support?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their elongated form and thick, lignified walls reinforce the tissue mechanically.

teacher_understanding.question: How does their main role differ from that of tracheids and vessels?
teacher_understanding.answer: Fibres mainly support, while tracheids and vessels are identified here with vertical transport of water and minerals.

items.exam_note: A frequent component–function matching distinction; retain 'mainly'.
